html:
The imperial dynasty that ruled China from 202 BCE to 220 CE, with a break from 9 to 23 CE. It was founded by Liu Bang, a commoner who won the civil war that followed the fall of the Qin. Its time is remembered as a golden age, and most Chinese still call themselves Han people.

The Han kept the Qin's centralised state but softened it. The empire was split into commanderies run by appointed officials and kingdoms given to relatives, which lost their power over time. From Emperor Wu (reigned 141 to 87 BCE) the court backed the teachings of Confucius, and scholars trained in the classics came to run the government.

Its reach and its works:

  • Emperor Wu fought the Xiongnu and pushed west into Central Asia, helping open the Silk Road.
  • Sima Qian wrote the first great history of China.
  • Cai Lun improved papermaking, and Zhang Heng built a seismoscope.
  • A census of 2 CE counted almost 60 million people, about the size of the Roman Empire at the same time.

The two empires knew of each other only dimly; a group claiming to come from Rome reached the Han court in 166.

The dynasty is split in two. The Western Han ruled from Chang'an until the regent Wang Mang seized the throne. The Eastern Han, restored in 25 CE, ruled from Luoyang. Court factions, eunuchs and the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184 broke its power, and generals carved up the land into the Three Kingdoms, the start of a long period of division.
